title: How Jason Cohen won loyal customers by being honest about being a one-man company
summary: Jason Cohen tells how an early customer, Tom, put up with a buggy first product and drove a big enterprise order because Jason was honest about being a one-person shop. Early adopters want to take part in building the product, and pretending to be bigger than you are loses the people who would have loved you as you are.

principles.text: Customers forgive honest mistakes from earnest people, not from cold corporations.
principles.quote: Customers love you when you're honest, even about your foibles. We forgive honest mistakes from earnest people, not stolid, cold, inhuman corporations.

principles.text: When a customer sees through your facade and accepts you anyway, match their honesty instead of going defensive.
principles.quote: Tom was saying: "I know who you really are, and I accept it. I still want to do this. How about a few features since we put up with those bugs?" I *had* to match that honesty.

principles.text: A customer who champions you inside their company stakes their own reputation on you, so keep your word and make them look good.
principles.quote: So he pinned his own reputation on it and won. As a bonus, he lived vicariously through Smart Bear as a product designer.

principles.text: Your first hundred customers are early adopters who want to shape the product and say they were there at the start.
principles.quote: they'll be early-adopters--folks who like trying new stuff and like working with new companies who still have spark and something to prove. Folks who want to be part of the creative process

principles.text: Pretending to be something you're not betrays the people who would have loved the real you.
principles.quote: If you pretend to be something you're not, they'll see right through it. Then what have you done? You've lied to those who would have loved you for who you are

principles.text: Honesty is a real advantage small companies have over big ones, so use it.
principles.quote: And it's one of the few advantages small companies have over big ones. Use it.
